registros.descripcion: Followup for chronic postoperative ankle pain, dyslipidemia, sleep apnea, and preventive care.
registros.texto_generado:
Sample Name: General Medicine Followup - Chronic Ankle Pain

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Followup for chronic postoperative ankle pain, dyslipidemia, sleep apnea, and preventive care.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: This is a 48-year-old male seen for routine followup. He sustained a left ankle fracture in 1988 and reports seven subsequent operations. Chronic ankle pain persists with episodic instability and falls. He previously used Vicodin only for severe pain but has run out; he also uses naproxen as needed. As a truck driver with unpredictable shifts lasting up to 14 hours, he avoids sedating medications while driving. He reports using CPAP after a sleep study with improved sleep. He has been working on dietary changes and has limited opportunities to exercise. His weight has decreased from approximately 330 to 310 pounds. He reports a prior outside evaluation for increased iron levels and possible fatty liver on ultrasonography.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Dyslipidemia, sleep apnea, obesity, and chronic left ankle pain following fracture and multiple procedures. Possible previous elevated iron levels and fatty liver, by patient report.

MEDICATIONS: Intermittent naproxen and previously Vicodin for pain; aspirin taken for pain. Medication reconciliation was discussed.

SOCIAL HISTORY: The patient drives a truck with irregular on-call hours. He has never smoked.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS: No new complaints apart from chronic ankle symptoms. The patient reports occasional giving way of the ankle.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Blood pressure was described as satisfactory. There is localized ankle tenderness and chronic mild swelling on examination. No numerical vital signs were provided.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Chronic left ankle pain following multiple surgeries. Trial of Norco for severe pain as needed; naproxen 500 mg twice daily as needed was renewed. Sedation, renal risks, and avoidance of analgesics when unnecessary were discussed, particularly given his driving occupation.
2. Dyslipidemia. LDL was 136. Diet and exercise counseling was provided; no new lipid-lowering medication was documented.
3. Obesity and sleep apnea. Encouraged further gradual weight reduction and continued CPAP use.
4. History of elevated iron and possible fatty liver. Iron studies were requested as an add-on to the blood already drawn, with notification of abnormal results planned. Hemochromatosis was discussed as a possible explanation, not an established diagnosis.
5. Preventive care. The patient declined influenza vaccination and preferred to defer Tdap. He reported a preference for do-not-resuscitate status and was instructed to submit his advance directive documentation for the medical record.

Followup in approximately one year, or sooner if needed.

registros.titulo: General Medicine Followup - Dysuria and Knee Pain
registros.descripcion: Evaluation of urinary burning and frequency, intermittent knee pain following a fall, and medication-related tremulousness.
registros.texto_generado:
Sample Name: General Medicine Followup - Dysuria and Knee Pain

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Evaluation of urinary burning and frequency, intermittent knee pain following a fall, and medication-related tremulousness.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient returns with approximately two weeks of discomfort on urination and increased urinary frequency. He has chronic prostate-related symptoms and reports nocturia, recently two to three times nightly, previously more frequent while taking his diuretic at night. A companion assists with the history and medication review. The patient also reports episodic sharp knee pain after falling from a chair. There was bruising but no significant swelling, and the pain is intermittent rather than consistently related to weight bearing. A companion describes episodes of marked shaking while he holds a cup. The patient uses albuterol approximately once daily and takes Depakote; he also drinks coffee and sometimes takes medication without breakfast. He was not shaking during the visit. Medication lists included duplicate prescriptions, although the clinician determined that these did not necessarily represent double dosing.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Chronic urinary or prostate symptoms, chronic knee complaints, and additional conditions treated with albuterol and Depakote. The patient reports using CPAP.

MEDICATIONS: Medication reconciliation was performed. Albuterol and Depakote, reportedly 1500 mg at night, were discussed. Other medications were renewed as needed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Dysuria and urinary frequency. Urinalysis and urine testing were requested. Because of the clinical suspicion for urinary infection, an empiric 10-day antibiotic course was prescribed. The patient was instructed to complete the full course and return if symptoms persisted after treatment.
2. Intermittent knee pain following a fall. No convincing fracture was identified clinically; a contemplated x-ray was not pursued. Tylenol as needed was prescribed for discomfort.
3. Episodic tremulousness. Potential contributors include albuterol, caffeine, and taking medication without food. The cause was not definitively established. Regular meals and taking appropriate medications with food were discussed.
4. Elevated blood glucose readings. Blood work including glycemic assessment, electrolytes, blood counts, and lipids was arranged. Diabetes treatment would depend on the results; a new diagnosis or medication was not confirmed during this discussion.
5. Chronic conditions and medication management. Prescriptions requiring renewal were addressed, with review of duplicate entries.

Laboratory testing was to be completed after the visit, with telephone notification if treatment changes were required. Followup in six months, or earlier if the urinary symptoms failed to improve.

registros.descripcion: Evaluation of symptomatic low home blood glucose readings in an older patient taking diabetes medication.
registros.texto_generado:
Sample Name: General Medicine Followup - Low Blood Glucose

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Evaluation of symptomatic low home blood glucose readings in an older patient taking diabetes medication.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: An 86-year-old gentleman with diabetes and hypertension presents because he suspects that his diabetes medication is causing fatigue and dizziness. He has taken it inconsistently and forgot it during a six-day trip. While off treatment, home glucose readings were reportedly in the 90 to 101 range. After taking his medication, he recorded glucose as low as 49. He has been modifying his diet to reduce starches and is concerned about whether he still requires diabetes treatment. He continues to take several antihypertensive medicines but is uncertain of some names and doses. He also discusses erectile difficulties and asks whether these may be related to a blood pressure medication. He describes recent cold symptoms and has a scheduled eye clinic appointment. Previous operations on both eyes were reported. He has poor dentition and is reluctant to obtain dental care.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Diabetes mellitus and hypertension. History of ophthalmic surgery.

MEDICATIONS: Metformin, taken intermittently before this visit; multiple antihypertensives, incompletely identified.

SOCIAL HISTORY: Former smoker, quit approximately 15 years previously.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS: Dizziness and tiredness temporally associated by the patient with his diabetes tablets. No chest pain or dyspnea was elicited during the visit.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Diabetes mellitus with reported hypoglycemia. Given repeated low readings including a value of 49, the patient was repeatedly instructed to stop metformin for now. Repeat laboratory testing was ordered, with further medication decisions to be based on the results. The importance of addressing symptomatic low glucose was discussed.
2. Hypertension. Medication review was performed and required prescriptions renewed; the patient was advised to continue the other agreed medications.
3. Erectile difficulties. The patient requested medication and expressed concern about antihypertensive side effects. No new treatment for erectile dysfunction was clearly documented.
4. Eye and dental care. Continue scheduled ophthalmology followup. Dental assessment and possible dentures were recommended in view of poor dentition.

The patient was asked to obtain laboratory testing and collect prescriptions, with further followup to be arranged according to results.

registros.descripcion: Followup after negative sexually transmitted infection testing, with review of blood pressure, glucose control, and cardiovascular medications.
registros.texto_generado:
Sample Name: General Medicine Followup - Hypertension and Diabetes

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Followup after negative sexually transmitted infection testing, with review of blood pressure, glucose control, and cardiovascular medications.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient was previously evaluated in urgent care for urethral burning or discharge. He states that these symptoms have resolved. HIV, syphilis, gonorrhea, and Chlamydia testing were reported as negative. He continues terazosin for urinary or prostate symptoms with nocturia. He drinks considerable sweetened lemonade, including in the evening. He has coronary artery disease treated with a coronary stent and has diabetes and hypertension. He stopped taking his blood pressure medication for approximately one month because home readings seemed low, and his home cuff recently stopped functioning. Clinic blood pressure today is 135/74. His last hemoglobin A1c in December was 6.4, improved from approximately 7. He takes metformin and would prefer to use fewer medicines. He reports adherence to aspirin and Plavix. His blood counts have declined somewhat compared with previous measurements, and he asks whether he may donate blood.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Coronary artery disease status post stent placement, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and prostate-related urinary symptoms.

MEDICATIONS: Metformin, terazosin, aspirin, Plavix, and previously prescribed antihypertensives including lisinopril; metoprolol was also discussed.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Blood pressure 135/74. No chest pain or shortness of breath was reported.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Hypertension in the setting of coronary artery disease and diabetes. Restart low-dose lisinopril, described at the conclusion of the visit as one-half tablet daily. Home blood pressure monitoring and a repeat office check in two weeks were arranged. The patient was asked to bring his monitor for comparison.
2. Type 2 diabetes, currently well controlled by A1c. A home glucometer was ordered. Record fasting or two-hour postprandial readings several times weekly. A trial off metformin could be considered if subsequent values remain satisfactory; discontinuation was not ordered at this visit.
3. Coronary artery disease. The importance of continuing aspirin and Plavix after stenting was emphasized.
4. Mild decline in blood count. Repeat CBC ordered before clearance for blood donation.
5. Resolved urethral symptoms. Reviewed negative sexually transmitted infection results and advised safe sexual practices. Continue terazosin and reduce late-evening fluid intake for nocturia.

Return in two weeks for blood pressure reassessment.

registros.descripcion: Medication review and followup for gait imbalance, nocturnal gastroesophageal reflux, and constipation.
registros.texto_generado:
Sample Name: General Medicine Followup - Parkinson Disease and Reflux

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Medication review and followup for gait imbalance, nocturnal gastroesophageal reflux, and constipation.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: An older patient with Parkinson disease presents for an extended review of medications and ongoing symptoms. Tremor is relatively controllable, but balance and walking have become more difficult. Followup with neurology and physical therapy were discussed. The patient has bothersome reflux predominantly at night, awakening around 11:30 p.m. with throat burning despite raising the head of the bed. Symptoms have been persistent for several months, with a history of antireflux surgery approximately ten years previously and recurrent symptoms for several years. He is taking several gastrointestinal medications, including omeprazole and sucralfate. Sucralfate has been associated with constipation, for which he has used polyethylene glycol, fiber, and occasional laxative therapy. He is intentionally losing weight and uses nighttime positive airway pressure for sleep apnea. He denies chest pain and significant shortness of breath during the discussion.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Parkinson disease, gastroesophageal reflux disease, constipation, hypertension, thyroid disease, and sleep apnea.

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY: Previous antireflux surgery, by history.

MEDICATIONS: Extensive medication reconciliation included neurologic therapy, furosemide, thyroid medication, omeprazole, sucralfate, polyethylene glycol, and melatonin. Specific doses were not consistently established in the conversation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Refractory nocturnal gastroesophageal reflux. Stop omeprazole and begin pantoprazole twice daily, approximately 30 minutes before breakfast and dinner. Gastroenterology referral was placed for consideration of further evaluation, given recurrent symptoms despite treatment and prior surgery.
2. Parkinson disease with gait and balance complaints. Continue neurologic followup and physical therapy; no new neurologic medication adjustment was clearly established.
3. Constipation, possibly aggravated by sucralfate. Bowel regimen was discussed, including a daily stool softener and review of laxative use.
4. Chronic medical management. Medication list reviewed and refills arranged as needed. An INR blood test requested by another clinician could not be added to the earlier sample, so a new draw was ordered.

Followup in approximately six months.

registros.descripcion: Followup of daytime fatigue, recurrent low blood glucose, hypertension, sleep apnea, and resumed alcohol consumption.
registros.texto_generado:
Sample Name: General Medicine Followup - Fatigue and Diabetes

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Followup of daytime fatigue, recurrent low blood glucose, hypertension, sleep apnea, and resumed alcohol consumption.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient reports significant daytime lethargy and frequent sleep despite taking Adderall three times daily. His medication regimen includes psychiatric therapy and intermittent trazodone for sleep. He resumed drinking alcohol approximately three months ago after two and a half years of abstinence. He has difficulty adhering to CPAP therapy and has also gained weight and been less active. He takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily for diabetes but frequently skips meals and reports approximately eight or nine glucose readings in the 40s or 50s, sometimes requiring glucose tablets. Morning readings are otherwise often around the 140s. He also takes lisinopril and metoprolol for hypertension but did not take his scheduled doses on the day of evaluation. He requests further help with alcohol use and psychosocial problems.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, psychiatric symptoms treated by a psychiatrist, and history of alcohol misuse.

MEDICATIONS: Metformin, lisinopril, metoprolol, Adderall, trazodone as needed, and other psychiatric medications. Ativan was discussed in relation to alcohol. Simvastatin was no longer being taken.

LABORATORY DATA: Recent review indicated normal blood counts, electrolytes, kidney and liver function. LDL was 31 and HDL 62.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Diabetes with recurrent hypoglycemia in the setting of missed meals. Emphasized regular breakfast, lunch, and dinner; do not take the corresponding metformin dose when not eating. Consider decreasing the evening metformin dose from 1000 mg to 500 mg. Seek prompt assessment for repeated symptomatic low readings.
2. Daytime somnolence and obstructive sleep apnea. Fatigue is likely multifactorial. Consistent CPAP use, activity, and weight management were encouraged. Psychiatric medications should be reviewed with his psychiatrist.
3. Return to alcohol use. Strongly advised cessation, psychological or addiction counseling, and avoidance of alcohol together with Ativan or trazodone. Psychology referral was placed.
4. Hypertension. Continue metoprolol and lisinopril; no adjustment was made because prescribed doses had been missed. Recheck blood pressure in two weeks.
5. Dyslipidemia. Lipid panel is favorable; simvastatin was removed from the medication list.
6. Erectile dysfunction. Levitra (vardenafil) was renewed as requested.

Followup for blood pressure in two weeks.

3. Preventive care. Influenza vaccination was discussed. Colonoscopy history was reviewed and repeat screening was not yet due by the clinician's assessment.

Description: Persistent intermittent blood pressure elevation despite multiple medications, with consideration of secondary causes.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient returns with his home blood pressure log and concerns about office measurements. He is currently treated with four antihypertensive agents and reports generally more favorable readings at home and at outside visits; recent outside values were approximately 128 to 135 systolic. In the office, systolic readings were reported at approximately 165 to 170. He is uncertain whether a previously proposed magnetic resonance angiogram of the renal arteries was already completed elsewhere. Renovascular disease has been raised as a possible secondary cause of difficult-to-control hypertension. He continues to smoke approximately six to eight cigarettes daily. He acknowledges longstanding snoring severe enough that his wife sleeps in another room, although he does not report substantial daytime sleepiness.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Hypertension requiring multiple drugs. Dyslipidemia and glucose measurements were reviewed and described as well controlled.

MEDICATIONS: Four blood pressure medications, including clonidine for which additional refills were requested; the complete regimen was not specified consistently.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Repeat clinic systolic blood pressure was approximately 170. No chest pain or shortness of breath was reported.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Difficult-to-control hypertension with variable home and clinic readings. Continue medication management and review the prior outside workup. A renal artery MRA will not be repeated until the clinician verifies whether it has already been done. The patient will request outside records or notify the clinic if no study exists.
2. Snoring and possible obstructive sleep apnea. A sleep study through the Pulmonary service was ordered as a potential investigation for a secondary contributor to hypertension.
3. Tobacco use. Smoking was reviewed and reduction or cessation encouraged.
4. Medications. Clonidine refill and other necessary renewals were addressed.

Followup in six months, or earlier if records or symptoms warrant further evaluation.

registros.descripcion: Evaluation of worsening heel pain attributed to plantar fasciitis, with routine preventive counseling.
registros.texto_generado:
Sample Name: Primary Care Consultation - Plantar Fasciitis

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Evaluation of worsening heel pain attributed to plantar fasciitis, with routine preventive counseling.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient recently attended the emergency department for a flare of previously recognized plantar fasciitis. Walking is painful, and he describes a balloon-like sensation in the heel with each step. The foot tends to be stiff in the morning and becomes progressively more painful during the day. He attempts to avoid heel pressure by walking on the ball of the foot and finds bicycle riding easier than walking. He brought previous x-ray reports. Podiatry followup was already scheduled for August 2. He is currently living in a rescue mission or homelessness program and has limited control over his diet and access to resources.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Recurrent plantar fasciitis. No additional established chronic illnesses were clearly identified during the interview.

SOCIAL HISTORY: Reports only brief cigarette use in childhood and no significant history of alcohol misuse. Currently engaged with the homeless services program.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: The foot and heel were examined; symptoms were predominantly associated with weight bearing and heel motion. The initial blood pressure was mildly elevated and was to be repeated. Weight placed the patient in the obese range, according to the clinician.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Plantar fasciitis. Recommended plantar stretching exercises, ice, and anti-inflammatory medication. Ibuprofen was preferred over the medication previously supplied in the emergency department, with instructions for use approximately every eight hours as needed. Attend the scheduled Podiatry appointment for further assessment, footwear recommendations, and possible additional studies. Contact the clinic if not improving.
2. Obesity. Encouraged activity as tolerated, particularly cycling, and dietary improvement. The MOVE weight-management program was discussed, recognizing limited dietary control in his living situation.
3. Preventive care. Screening colonoscopy was strongly encouraged and the procedure discussed. Advance directives and healthcare decision-making were reviewed, as the patient had concerns about having no designated surrogate.
4. Routine laboratory tests were ordered.

Return in approximately six months.

Sample Name: General Medicine Followup - Vitamin D Deficiency

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Followup of low vitamin D, occasional low heart rate, prior syncope, and osteoarthritis.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient returns doing generally well. An echocardiogram obtained at the end of January was normal by the clinician's review. He occasionally records a pulse around 52 at home and is concerned because he takes atenolol. He had a brief episode of syncope requiring hospital observation in February, which he associates with overheating; he has not described recurrent associated symptoms at this visit. Most recorded heart rates have been in the 60s and 70s. His blood pressure and lipid values were regarded as controlled. He has disabling knee osteoarthritis limiting walking distance and needs paperwork for renewal of his disability parking permit. A low vitamin D level was found on recent testing.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Hypertension or cardiovascular risk treated with atenolol, prior syncopal episode, knee osteoarthritis, and vitamin D insufficiency. History of colonoscopy with removal of polyps and continuing urology followup.

MEDICATIONS: Atenolol; over-the-counter vitamin D, approximately 800 units daily, before the new regimen.

LABORATORY DATA: Lipid results discussed included LDL 67. Vitamin D was borderline low. Other recent laboratory findings were not described as requiring a change in management.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Low vitamin D. Prescribe a concentrated vitamin D supplement once weekly for 12 weeks. Suspend the patient's routine supplement during this treatment and resume it after completion. Repeat vitamin D testing shortly before followup.
2. Intermittent relative bradycardia and prior syncope. The echocardiogram is reassuring. Continue low-dose atenolol if asymptomatic; with recurrent low pulse associated with dizziness or presyncope, hold the dose and seek timely reassessment.
3. Hypertension and lipid management. Continue existing therapy. Aerobic activity such as a stationary bicycle was recommended, given limited walking tolerance from knee pain.
4. Bilateral knee osteoarthritis. Disability parking documentation was reviewed.
5. Continue urology surveillance as scheduled.

Followup in approximately four months, after laboratory re-evaluation.

registros.descripcion: Review of diabetes therapy and cardiovascular medications after hospitalization for a rapid heart rhythm.
registros.texto_generado:
Sample Name: Medication Consultation - Diabetes and Renal Impairment

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Review of diabetes therapy and cardiovascular medications after hospitalization for a rapid heart rhythm.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient returns after a recent admission for tachyarrhythmia and changes to multiple medications. He has restarted Coumadin and is undergoing regular anticoagulation monitoring. Metformin was discontinued because of reduced renal function, after which blood glucose increased. He takes glipizide 10 mg twice daily, but morning glucose is now approximately 150 to 160 and evening readings approach 290. He reports some ankle edema. His heart rate is improved on the new regimen, but systolic blood pressures commonly reach the 140s to 150s. Higher lisinopril doses previously caused elevated potassium. He is concerned about medication risks and requests clarification of the discharge regimen.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Diabetes mellitus, hypertension, impaired renal function, and a recently treated rapid cardiac rhythm requiring anticoagulation. Possible previous volume overload was discussed, although the patient disputes having had heart failure.

MEDICATIONS: Coumadin, glipizide 10 mg twice daily, lisinopril, furosemide, and other rate-controlling or cardiovascular medications.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Heart rate 67 with regular rhythm at this visit. Blood pressure elevated. Mild right ankle swelling was reported.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Diabetes, inadequately controlled since metformin was discontinued for renal impairment. Continue glipizide and add pioglitazone once daily in the morning. Potential fluid retention and edema were discussed; insulin may be necessary if oral therapy remains inadequate. Do not restart metformin given kidney dysfunction.
2. Hypertension. Because increasing lisinopril may exacerbate hyperkalemia and the heart rate is already controlled, increase furosemide to twice daily. Monitor symptoms, renal function, and electrolytes.
3. Recent tachyarrhythmia and anticoagulation. Continue the prescribed cardiac regimen and Coumadin with scheduled INR monitoring. Bruising and bleeding risks were reviewed.

Obtain laboratory tests in approximately two weeks and follow up with the regular physician in about six weeks.

He reports exertional breathlessness and episodes of nocturnal cough relieved by albuterol. Exposure to dust and industrial grinding chemicals, as well as strong cologne, worsens breathing. His inhalers include Combivent, albuterol, and formoterol. He continues to smoke approximately one-half pack daily, having started in early adolescence. Nicotine patches are used intermittently, but he declines referral to a cessation clinic. Alcohol intake has decreased from approximately eight to four drinks weekly. He had previously experienced unintended weight loss, but weight is now stable. Earlier imaging performed during that evaluation was reportedly unrevealing apart from degenerative spinal changes. PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Chronic obstructive airways disease and prior evaluation for weight loss.

SOCIAL HISTORY: Active smoker; occupational exposure to respiratory irritants. Reports reduced alcohol intake.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS: Intermittent cough and exertional dyspnea. No new acute respiratory distress is documented at this visit.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Repeat blood pressure approximately 120/90. Other examination findings were not clearly quantified in the conversation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Obstructive lung disease with recent exacerbations. Continue maintenance and rescue inhalers, review correct use, and avoid dust, chemical exposure, and fragrances where possible. Pulmonary function testing remains indicated, but the patient requests that it be scheduled in January.
2. Tobacco dependence. Smoking cessation was discussed. The patient uses patches inconsistently and declines specialized cessation services at present.
3. Prior weight loss, currently stable. Previous workup was reviewed; continue monitoring.
4. Preventive care. Influenza vaccination and colorectal cancer screening were discussed. The patient declined colonoscopy.

Continue clinical followup and return sooner for worsening respiratory symptoms.

Description: Followup for intermittent hand locking, distal tingling, and chronic pain, with diabetes review.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient describes intermittent locking of the hands with tingling in the hands and feet. Symptoms are not present daily but appear worse in winter and with extremes of cold or heat. Pain has also increased. An unidentified medication used for neuropathic symptoms over the previous four months has been partially helpful. Electromyography and nerve conduction testing were previously discussed or requested but have been delayed for more than three months. Glucose readings at home have recently increased from approximately 125 to the 150s, occasionally reaching 180, without a clear dietary change. The patient has gained weight and walks less. Hemoglobin A1c in September was approximately 6%. The history also includes a remote bacterial corneal ulcer and corneal transplantation; cataract surgery is pending. The patient reports having received an influenza vaccine.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Diabetes mellitus, ocular disease with prior corneal ulcer and transplant, and cataract.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS: Intermittent distal paresthesias and hand locking. Chills were attributed by the patient to a cool home environment, with accompanying rhinorrhea.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Heart and lung sounds were described as normal. Sensation to touch was preserved on repeated testing.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Distal paresthesias, episodic hand locking, and pain of uncertain etiology. Neuropathic or cervical causes remain under evaluation; no definitive etiology was established. After discussion with another clinician, begin gabapentin 100 mg three times daily. A cervical spine MRI was arranged, possibly for the following day. Electrodiagnostic studies remain relevant but their exact scheduling was not confirmed.
2. Diabetes. Repeat laboratory testing was requested. Recent increased home readings, weight gain, and reduced physical activity were reviewed without a documented medication change.
3. Ophthalmic history. Continue planned cataract and specialist followup.

Laboratory studies today and general clinic followup in approximately four months.

Description: Evaluation of localized low back pain and right thumb pain with review of preventive care.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient presents for annual followup and medication renewal, reporting approximately three months of persistent localized lumbar pain. It is typically rated 3 to 4 out of 10 but can become severe with twisting, bending, or changing position. There is no clear radicular pain down the legs. He has a remote history of lumbar problems and continues to perform physical work despite discomfort. He also reports one to two months of right thumb pain when gripping or squeezing. He is uncertain whether this represents arthritis or a strain. He recently lost part of a toenail. He is followed by Endocrinology for a parathyroid disorder and has scheduled laboratory monitoring.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Parathyroid disorder, chronic musculoskeletal complaints, hemorrhoids, and reflux symptoms controlled with medication.

SOCIAL HISTORY: Former smoker, reports remaining abstinent.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Focal lumbar tenderness with pain reproduced by rotation and movement. Straight-leg maneuvers were not clearly suggestive of a radicular syndrome. Thumb grip strength was preserved; provocative carpal tunnel maneuvers were unrevealing, although localized thumb discomfort persisted. Partially detached toenail without signs of infection.

IMPRESSION AND PLAN:
1. Mechanical low back pain, possibly muscular or degenerative. Lumbar radiographs were ordered to assess for fracture or structural change. Acetaminophen was recommended as needed, and Flexeril was prescribed up to three times daily as needed for suspected spasm. The clinician expressed caution about ibuprofen in light of other medical considerations.
2. Right thumb pain, possibly degenerative joint disease. Right thumb or hand radiographs ordered. Conservative analgesia initially; reassess if persistent.
3. Detached toenail. No evidence of infection. Allow the remaining loose nail to separate naturally; regrowth may take time.
4. Preventive care. Zoster vaccination was recommended and to be scheduled separately. Routine endocrine laboratory testing remains due at the previously designated time.

The patient will be contacted for unexpected x-ray findings and return in six months or sooner for persistent symptoms.

Description: Assessment of new action-related hand tremor, nocturnal reflux, and persistent Grover disease symptoms.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient reports a gradually more noticeable tremulous movement, initially in the right hand, primarily when lifting a cup in the morning. He has little difficulty with other fine motor tasks, and there is no constant resting tremor described. He also experiences acid regurgitation when lying down after late meals, occurring several times during the preceding month. His chronic Grover disease remains intermittently pruritic despite treatment, and he asks about light therapy discussed with an acquaintance. SOCIAL HISTORY: Denies significant current alcohol or tobacco use.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Hand coordination and tremor were assessed during upper extremity examination; no definite neurologic diagnosis was established. Blood pressure was described as satisfactory.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Gastroesophageal reflux. Avoid meals close to bedtime and identify food triggers. Trial omeprazole once daily for approximately two to three months, with a plan to reassess and discontinue if symptoms resolve. Consider upper endoscopy for persistent or worsening reflux.
2. Mild intermittent action-related hand shaking. Symptoms and examination reviewed; no specific diagnosis or treatment was established at this time. Monitor progression.
3. Persistent Grover disease. Advised discussion with Dermatology regarding the potential role of phototherapy rather than initiating it through primary care.
4. Preventive care. Arrange zoster vaccination at a subsequent nursing visit. Review previous colonoscopy records to determine whether repeat screening is indicated. Fasting laboratory testing including lipids was requested.
5. Routine medications. Renew appropriate prescriptions and discontinue inactive entries after reconciliation.

Followup after several months or earlier for worsening symptoms.

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Persistent unilateral arm pain and electrical sensations, with chronic lumbar spinal stenosis.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient returns with persistent intermittent discomfort in one arm, described as electrical pain and perceived swelling. The symptoms began several weeks after a fall in which the arm or shoulder struck a wall. They are provoked by certain arm positions, grooming, and shaving and may improve when the neck is turned or the arm is repositioned. He reports no associated loss of strength. Previously ordered electrodiagnostic testing was canceled and has not yet been rescheduled. He also has established lumbar spinal stenosis with back pain on standing or walking and relief after movement or changes in position. Acetaminophen provides limited symptomatic benefit.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Lumbar spinal stenosis and chronic back pain.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Upper extremity strength was preserved and comparable bilaterally on grip, pushing, and pulling. Shoulder movement did not consistently reproduce pain. Position-related symptoms raised concern for irritation of a peripheral nerve or cervical nerve pathway; the precise site was not determined.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Unilateral arm pain with neuropathic features. Reschedule the previously canceled nerve conduction/electrodiagnostic study. The cause may involve neural irritation after the fall, but localization and diagnosis are uncertain. After discussion with the supervising clinician, begin low-dose desipramine at bedtime for neuropathic pain, advising that relief may take one to two weeks and that sedation is possible. Continue tolerated acetaminophen for breakthrough pain.
2. Lumbar spinal stenosis. Chronic symptoms were reviewed. Continue conservative management while tolerable; invasive options were discussed only in general terms.
3. Medication renewals were arranged where needed.

Return in approximately two months to review testing and response to treatment.

registros.descripcion: Review of an indeterminate prostate biopsy, thrombocytopenia with hepatic findings, and blood pressure management.
registros.texto_generado:
Sample Name: General Medicine Followup - Prostate Biopsy and Hypertension

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Review of an indeterminate prostate biopsy, thrombocytopenia with hepatic findings, and blood pressure management.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient presents for followup after a prostate biopsy and recent laboratory work. He was informed that the tissue showed cells suspicious for adenocarcinoma but that a definitive cancer diagnosis was not established in the explanation given at this visit. Urology documentation suggested repeat PSA and biopsy in approximately one year, while the patient recalls being told to return in six months. He also has persistent thrombocytopenia under evaluation, with reports of an enlarged spleen, hepatomegaly, and fatty liver. Previous alcohol use may contribute, but the etiology has not been settled. A liver biopsy has been discussed but not completed. Morning systolic blood pressure at home is often 140 to 150. Most other complaints are stable; previously bothersome joint pain has improved following therapy.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Hypertension, coronary disease by history, thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly with fatty liver, and prostate abnormality under surveillance. The patient relates a history of major abdominal surgery and prior myocardial events.

MEDICATIONS: Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, lisinopril 10 mg, metoprolol 25 mg, and other chronic prescriptions.

LABORATORY DATA: Hemoglobin A1c approximately 6.1, previously in the 5% range. Platelets remained low. Cholesterol was regarded as satisfactory.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Indeterminate prostate biopsy suspicious for malignancy. Continue Urology followup and clarify the interval for repeat PSA and possible biopsy; avoid labeling the finding as proven prostate carcinoma.
2. Thrombocytopenia with splenomegaly and fatty liver. Continue specialist evaluation. The clinician advised followup with the liver service about whether the previously considered biopsy is required.
3. Hypertension with elevated morning readings. Increase lisinopril from 10 to 20 mg daily; continue hydrochlorothiazide and metoprolol.
4. Mild increase in A1c. Review diet and continue metabolic monitoring.
5. Medication reconciliation and appropriate prescription renewals were completed. Future colonoscopy surveillance was discussed.

Return for routine followup in approximately six months.

registros.descripcion: Review of multiple antihypertensive medications, chronic back pain, weight reduction, and sleep apnea.

Sample Name: General Medicine Followup - Hypertension and Medication Review

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Review of multiple antihypertensive medications, chronic back pain, weight reduction, and sleep apnea.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient returns for medication reconciliation. He has been exercising at a fitness facility and is pleased with recent weight reduction to approximately 277 to 278 pounds. He has chronic back pain following injury, for which he intermittently uses gabapentin, cyclobenzaprine, and acetaminophen. He ran out of gabapentin. He is also confused by overlapping prescriptions and extra bottles of simvastatin received in the mail. His home systolic blood pressure is commonly around 140. He has been taking hydralazine only once in the morning rather than twice daily. He has a remote history of a reported myocardial infarction and continues to smoke intermittently when stressed. Obstructive sleep apnea was previously diagnosed, but he finds his old CPAP machine uncomfortable and has not been using it consistently.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Hypertension treated with multiple medications, coronary disease or previous myocardial infarction by history, chronic back pain, obesity, and obstructive sleep apnea.

MEDICATIONS: Lisinopril, amlodipine, hydralazine, hydrochlorothiazide-containing treatment, simvastatin, gabapentin, cyclobenzaprine, and intermittent acetaminophen. Doses and usage were reconciled.

LABORATORY DATA: Blood counts, PSA, and aldosterone investigation for secondary hypertension were described as normal.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Hypertension. Reviewed dosing schedule and advised hydralazine twice daily, once in the morning and once in the afternoon, rather than the patient's once-daily use. Continue the remaining prescribed blood pressure regimen and reassess as weight decreases.
2. Chronic back pain. Renew gabapentin and cyclobenzaprine as needed, and review other analgesics.
3. Obesity. Continue supervised exercise and weight-loss efforts.
4. Obstructive sleep apnea. Encouraged consistent CPAP and offered reassessment or trial of a more comfortable interface through Sleep Clinic; patient remained reluctant.
5. Remote coronary disease. Prior metoprolol and Plavix use was reviewed; no definite new cardiovascular medication was added.
6. Tobacco use. Smoking cessation services were discussed.

Repeat relevant laboratory testing before followup in approximately three months.

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Followup after hospitalization for symptomatic skipped heartbeats, with medication and screening review.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient reports a recent two-day hospital observation for a sensation of skipped heartbeats accompanied by nausea. A subsequent ambulatory monitor, worn for approximately one month, did not capture further symptoms according to the patient. He describes a similar episode about a year previously. Known coronary artery blockages have been treated medically because intervention with stents was reportedly not feasible. He takes Ranexa and inquires about obtaining it through this clinic because of its cost. Home blood pressure varies; the clinic reading today is 132/80. He needs additional home glucose test strips and a routine diabetes and cholesterol assessment. Right cataract extraction approximately two months ago improved his vision; surgery for the opposite eye is anticipated.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Coronary artery disease with medically managed stenoses, episodic perceived arrhythmia, diabetes, hypertension, and cataracts.

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY: Recent right cataract extraction.

SOCIAL HISTORY: Former smoker who quit almost 50 years ago.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Blood pressure 132/80. The patient is comfortable and describes no ongoing episode of palpitations during the visit.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Coronary disease with recent intermittent palpitations and hospital evaluation. Continue specialist-directed medical therapy and Cardiology followup. Ranexa was not available on the routine formulary; a special request would require Cardiology approval, but the patient elected to continue his present supply.
2. Diabetes mellitus. Refill glucose test strips. Obtain hemoglobin A1c with followup blood work.
3. Hyperlipidemia. Schedule a fasting lipid profile, as the patient had eaten before today's visit.
4. Hypertension. Blood pressure was close to the clinician's target; continue monitoring and existing treatment.
5. Cataracts. Continue Ophthalmology care for the planned contralateral procedure.

Return in six months and obtain the ordered fasting studies in the meantime.

registros.descripcion: Followup for severe chronic spinal pain and concerns about prior pain-management injections and medications.

Sample Name: Chronic Pain Consultation - Lumbar and Cervical Pain

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Followup for severe chronic spinal pain and concerns about prior pain-management injections and medications.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient presents with persistent severe chronic lumbar and neck pain, reporting that a recent injection at the Pain Clinic increased rather than relieved pain. Earlier procedures had been more helpful. He is dissatisfied with repeated changes in clinic personnel and requests evaluation by a different pain specialist. He has previously taken Vicodin and occasional morphine 15 mg for severe episodes and has used gabapentin but does not wish to continue it. The patient is uncomfortable with being referred to psychiatric care for a physical pain complaint. He acknowledges stress but does not consider himself depressed. He also reports positional exacerbation of neck and back pain. Prior MRI studies of the lumbar and cervical spine were reviewed; repeat imaging was not felt necessary at this encounter.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Chronic severe lumbar and cervical pain with documented spinal degenerative or narrowing changes. Long-term analgesic use.

MEDICATIONS: Vicodin, intermittent morphine 15 mg, previous gabapentin, and other chronic medications. An earlier recommendation for amitriptyline had not been accepted or understood.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Chronic lumbar and cervical pain, with incomplete response to injections and medications. Submit a new Pain Clinic referral, noting the patient's request for a different physician and possible repeat intervention. Reviewed the previous spinal MRI rather than ordering another immediately.
2. Possible neuropathic component. Discussed why amitriptyline may be used for nerve pain independent of its antidepressant classification. A trial of a very low nighttime dose was prescribed after the patient agreed to consider it. Sedation and delayed onset of effect were discussed.
3. Chronic opioid use. Previous Vicodin and intermittent morphine use were reviewed. Prescription needs were addressed with emphasis on specialist followup; the dialogue did not clearly establish a new escalation of opioid dosing.
4. Continue conservative exercises and observation for new neurologic or bowel/bladder symptoms.

Followup through the Pain Clinic and primary care as arranged.

registros.descripcion: Counseling about advanced hepatic fibrosis after unsuccessful hepatitis C treatment, with diabetes and eye care review.

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Counseling about advanced hepatic fibrosis after unsuccessful hepatitis C treatment, with diabetes and eye care review.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient reports that hepatitis C therapy was unsuccessful and that a liver biopsy and imaging were interpreted as showing advanced cirrhosis. He is anxious about prognosis, liver function, and the possibility of transplantation. He describes episodic severe fatigue and asks whether this relates to hepatic disease, diabetes, or treatment effects. The clinician reviewed the distinction between extensive scarring and current liver function, noting that recent blood tests suggested some preservation of hepatic function and no obvious jaundice. He also has diabetes treated with insulin glargine and metformin. Home glucose values are approximately 115 to 120; the prior A1c was 5.7. The patient reports early glaucoma and dry eyes requiring replacement drops. He has chronic pain and asks about cannabinoid-derived medication, but no such prescription was established.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Chronic hepatitis C with reported advanced cirrhosis after unsuccessful treatment, diabetes mellitus, glaucoma, chronic pain, and prior chest pain with reassuring stress evaluation.

MEDICATIONS: Insulin glargine approximately 25 units daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, low-dose aspirin, and nitroglycerin as needed. Other previously prescribed medicines were reconciled.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: No visible jaundice was described. Lungs were clear on auscultation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Chronic hepatitis C and cirrhosis. Discussed possible complications, surveillance, and transplantation considerations without declaring a specific prognosis or transplant eligibility. Repeat hepatitis C viral studies and liver function tests in approximately six months, with sooner evaluation for clinical deterioration.
2. Diabetes, well controlled by prior measurements. Continue current insulin and metformin regimen and repeat A1c and renal testing.
3. Glaucoma and dry eyes. Continue regular Ophthalmology surveillance and renew lubricating eye drops as appropriate.
4. Chronic pain and mood concerns. Discussion of alternative symptom management and Mental Health consultation; a cannabinoid medication was not prescribed.

Renew necessary medicines and return in approximately six months.

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Followup after emergency evaluation for chest and arm discomfort, with dyspnea, cough, and medication lapses.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient presents after an emergency department evaluation approximately two weeks ago for chest and arm pain, during which admission was advised but declined after the discomfort subsided. He continues to describe intermittent left arm pain, at times accompanied by chest pressure or stabbing discomfort, exertional breathlessness, headache, and a cough of about three months' duration. The cough is mostly dry but occasionally productive. He has diabetes, a history of an abnormal cardiac stress test, and several cardiovascular risk factors. Access to medications has been inconsistent; he is running out of clopidogrel, metoprolol, glipizide, and metformin. He reports taking approximately 18 units of insulin daily, with some readings in the high 100s. He stopped smoking almost two years ago. Lisinopril use was reviewed as a potential contributor to chronic cough.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia or coronary risk, and previous abnormal stress testing.

MEDICATIONS: Insulin, glipizide, metformin, lisinopril, metoprolol, clopidogrel, and other chronic therapy.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Intermittent chest discomfort, left arm pain, and dyspnea. Current symptoms were not judged to establish an acute infarction, but coronary disease and possible angina remain concerns. Cardiology reevaluation requested, with possible angiography depending on assessment. The patient was advised to follow through promptly with this appointment.
2. Left arm discomfort may be musculoskeletal; trial acetaminophen and ice while cardiac causes are evaluated.
3. Chronic cough. Obtain a two-view chest radiograph. Postnasal drainage and ACE inhibitor cough were considered. A nasal spray was prescribed, and the clinician planned to replace lisinopril with another antihypertensive less likely to cause cough.
4. Hypertension and diabetes. Medication renewal and intensified blood pressure treatment, including possible hydrochlorothiazide, were discussed. Laboratory studies requested; maintain prescribed diabetes therapy and monitor glucose.

Return in approximately three months, with earlier assessment for recurrent or worsening cardiopulmonary symptoms.

Sample Name: General Medicine Followup - Diabetes and Myalgias

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Review of muscle pain after high-dose statin use, fluctuating glucose, and coronary artery disease.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient reports an emergency department visit for generalized aching, chills, and bilateral shoulder and arm pain. He was advised to stop simvastatin 80 mg because a medication-related muscle reaction was suspected. Symptoms have substantially decreased but occasionally recur, often at rest. He has a history of coronary artery stenting, with two stents placed after angiography in 2010, and has a scheduled cardiology visit. Walking rapidly produces some dyspnea, but he does not report typical exertional chest pain. He takes insulin 36 units twice daily and describes wide glucose fluctuations, including values near 80 and others above 230, with occasional symptomatic lows. Recent A1c values have been approximately 6.9 to 7.3. He continues to experience bilateral knee discomfort.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Coronary artery disease after stenting, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and chronic knee pain.

MEDICATIONS: Aspirin, Plavix, amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, losartan, metoprolol, insulin, gemfibrozil, and other chronic medications. Simvastatin 80 mg was stopped after the emergency assessment.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Initial blood pressure approximately 173/80, with repeat 140/68. Foot sensation was assessed during the visit.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Possible statin-associated myalgias. Restart simvastatin at the lower dose of 20 mg rather than 80 mg. Discontinue if the severe muscle symptoms recur and contact the clinic.
2. Diabetes with variable home glucose. Increase morning insulin from 36 to 38 units while maintaining 36 units in the evening. Record fasting and postprandial readings and repeat fasting laboratory testing before followup.
3. Coronary artery disease. Continue antiplatelet and cardiac medications. Discuss the shoulder symptoms and any dyspnea with Cardiology at the upcoming visit.
4. Hypertension. Continue established treatment and monitor pressures.

Return in six to eight weeks, with fasting blood work beforehand.

Description: Evaluation of progressive ankle and foot discomfort, localized redness, and numbness in a patient with diabetes.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient reports longstanding intermittent ankle swelling after an injury sustained in military service, but over recent months swelling has become more persistent. There has been sharper pain, numbness, and discoloration or redness in the affected foot over the past several weeks. He describes a pins-and-needles sensation and notes difficulty maintaining his usual exercise because of work hours and discomfort. Diabetes control has been variable; an A1c in June was approximately 8%, while a more recent outside value was reported as 7.4. Fasting glucose is often in the 120s but may rise later in the day. He uses substantial insulin doses and has previously experienced nocturnal low glucose with mealtime insulin. Gabapentin was tried before but may have caused side effects.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Diabetes mellitus, remote ankle injury, and previous podiatric care.

MEDICATIONS: Insulin regimen including approximately 50 units in the morning and 55 at night, additional mealtime insulin as used by the patient, metformin, pravastatin, and previous gabapentin.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Localized erythema, warmth, tightness, and tenderness over the affected foot or ankle. Areas of peeling and cracked skin suggested possible fungal involvement. No purulent drainage was described. Sensory testing was performed.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Foot cellulitis in a patient with diabetes. Begin Keflex for seven days. The affected area was marked to help assess spread or regression. Recheck with nursing in one week; the patient should return earlier if the infection worsens.
2. Possible fungal skin involvement. Keep feet clean and dry, avoid walking barefoot, and discuss antifungal treatment after the acute infection improves; treatment for fungus was deferred today.
3. Neuropathic pain and paresthesias. Restart gabapentin at a low dose, with gradual dose adjustment through the primary physician if tolerated.
4. Diabetes. Reinforced consistent meals, glucose monitoring, and tighter glucose control to support healing.

Nursing reassessment in one week and routine followup with the primary care clinician.

Description: Assessment of worsening memory and behavioral fluctuations, with family discussion of home-based care.

2. Increasing care needs. Referral for Home-Based Primary Care and associated nursing or physical therapy support was initiated; availability and family approval remain to be confirmed.
3. Chronic respiratory disease. Renew albuterol and ipratropium nebulizer solutions and other necessary inhaler supplies.
4. Review blood pressure, hydration, pending B12 testing, and any minor electrolyte abnormalities during followup.

Continue care coordination with family and home health providers.

registros.descripcion: Medication reconciliation and supply renewals in a patient with diabetes, renal disease, and prior surgeries.

Description: Medication reconciliation and supply renewals in a patient with diabetes, renal disease, and prior surgeries.

4. Complex medication and equipment needs. Renew requested prescriptions for later use but ship only supplies currently required, including selected insulin and testing materials. Review ostomy or urinary drainage supplies.

Followup in several months.

registros.texto_generado:
Sample Name: General Medicine Followup - Cirrhosis with Edema

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Followup for hepatitis-associated cirrhosis, fluid retention, varices, and anticoagulation management.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient has advanced liver disease attributed to hepatitis, with known gastrointestinal varices and intermittent encephalopathy. A followup upper endoscopy is scheduled through an outside liver clinic to reassess varices. His INR is presently low after Coumadin doses were held under anticoagulation-clinic instructions for the procedure. He has significant chronic edema with intermittent leg blisters and acknowledges frequently missing prescribed diuretics because urinary frequency interferes with daily activities. He has limited mobility after a previous stroke and uses a scooter; the equipment lift is malfunctioning. He requests assistance with home chores and medication management. The hepatology service has not resumed interferon treatment and continues liver surveillance.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Hepatitis-related cirrhosis, gastric or esophageal varices, episodic hepatic encephalopathy, prior stroke with limited mobility, chronic edema, and ongoing anticoagulation.

MEDICATIONS: Coumadin managed with an anticoagulation clinic, diuretics including spironolactone or other water pills, lactulose, and previously prescribed lipid-lowering treatment.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Cirrhosis with varices. Continue hepatology management, scheduled endoscopy, and imaging and liver laboratory surveillance. Anticoagulation management around the procedure remains with the established team; the clinician did not specify a new independent Coumadin schedule.
2. Fluid retention and blood pressure elevation. Reinforced daily adherence to prescribed diuretics and salt restriction. Strategies for remembering medications were discussed.
3. Post-stroke disability and reduced independence. Physical and occupational therapy referrals and paperwork for assistance at home were addressed.
4. Hyperlipidemia. Resume the previously prescribed cholesterol treatment and obtain fasting labs with the next INR testing.
5. Additional evaluation. A bone density study was ordered.

Return for reassessment in approximately three months.

Description: Follow-up for diabetes, congestive heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and difficulty obtaining medication refills.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient returns primarily because of persistent difficulty obtaining refills through the pharmacy. Several medications have not arrived despite repeated requests, and he brings multiple bottles for review. He has not taken isosorbide dinitrate for approximately two to three months after running out. He continues hydralazine and other cardiovascular medications. He initially declines restarting the nitrate, partly because he wishes to use medication for erectile dysfunction, but agrees to consider taking it after discussion of its role in his heart failure regimen. He has not had new lower-extremity swelling. He also requests replacement nasal spray for nighttime congestion.

Regarding diabetes, he uses approximately 12 to 14 units of insulin at bedtime. He reports glucose falling into the 40s by morning unless he begins the night with a reading near 200 or eats overnight; fasting readings may otherwise be around 90 to 108. He is reluctant to add mealtime injections. Intermittent constipation and bleeding with straining are also discussed.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Congestive heart failure, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease with nephrology follow-up, anemia treated through nephrology, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and erectile dysfunction.

MEDICATIONS: Extensive reconciliation included insulin, hydralazine, isosorbide dinitrate, amlodipine, metoprolol, diuretics including Lasix, simvastatin, aspirin, gabapentin, pancreatic enzymes, iron, calcium with vitamin D, docusate, and senna. Availability and adherence vary because of refill difficulties.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: The patient is conversant. He denies current leg swelling, and recent podiatry examination was satisfactory. Heart and lungs were examined, without a clearly documented abnormal finding in the conversation.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Medication access and adherence. Medications were reviewed individually and refills renewed. Discussed the importance of continuity, particularly of the heart failure regimen. Isosorbide dinitrate was reordered during discussion, although the patient's willingness to continue it had fluctuated.
2. Diabetes with reported nocturnal hypoglycemia. Record fingerstick glucose three to four times daily for two weeks. Pharmacist visit in two weeks to review readings and adjust insulin as indicated; do not infer safe control from isolated fasting values.
3. Erectile dysfunction. Discussed the danger of sildenafil with nitrates and the concerns related to his cardiac status; sildenafil was not prescribed.
4. Nighttime nasal congestion. Flunisolide nasal spray prescribed.
5. Follow up in approximately three months, with an earlier pharmacist review.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Recovery after severe hospitalization. Reassurance regarding gradual recovery, with urgent reassessment for worsening symptoms.
2. Nephrolithiasis with ureteral stent and intermittent hematuria. Continue urologic follow-up for definitive management and stent removal. Return for heavy bleeding, dizziness, dyspnea, chest symptoms, or concern about significant blood loss.
3. Diabetes, currently tightly controlled. Medication timing and temporary holds were reviewed in light of current ciprofloxacin treatment and recent illness.
4. Hypertension and hyperlipidemia. Blood pressure and lipid profile are satisfactory; maintenance medications renewed.
5. Immunizations. Influenza and pneumococcal vaccines approved and arranged for administration at this visit.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Recurrent falls, possibly multifactorial, in the setting of neurologic ataxia and polypharmacy. Previous cardiac evaluation has not demonstrated a clear structural or arrhythmic cause. Obtain EKG and additional blood tests and review medications that may contribute. Support use of a wheelchair to reduce injury risk.
2. Bone protection after frequent falls. Check vitamin D and obtain DEXA scanning to assess for osteoporosis.
3. Swallowing difficulty. Continue precautions and follow-up of prior swallowing assessment; mixed consistencies and liquids can trigger coughing.
4. Medication refills were reviewed, including etodolac and allergy therapies. Patient reports penicillin and caffeine sensitivity.
5. Follow-up in three to four months, sooner for further injury, prolonged loss of consciousness, or worsening dysphagia.

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Evaluation of lower-extremity pain and paresthesias, questions about previously reported prostate cancer, and a recent episode of chest discomfort.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient presents with intermittent pain in the feet and legs, including numbness and tingling, and concern about the information he has received regarding a prostate cancer diagnosis or prostate testing at another facility. He is unsure what treatment, including radiation or surgery, may be planned, and seeks clarification. Much of his prior evaluation occurred at another medical center, and those records are not available during this encounter. He also recounts an episode of chest pain with sweating and arm symptoms lasting several minutes, without current recurrent pain. Cigarette consumption has decreased from previously heavy use but continues. He reports transient tingling and weakness in the arms during another episode.

EXAMINATION: Routine cardiopulmonary, neurologic, and lower-extremity examination was performed; no definitive etiology of the leg symptoms was established. An EKG was arranged because of recent chest pain.

IMPRESSION AND PLAN:
1. Reported prostate cancer or abnormal prostate testing. Definitive findings and stage cannot be confirmed from the current information. Follow up with the treating urologists at the original facility to review records, prognosis, and available treatments before making decisions.
2. Distal foot pain and paresthesias. Recommend evaluation of thyroid function, iron studies, and relevant vitamin deficiencies; written suggested tests provided for completion with his usual care team.
3. Recent chest pain with diaphoresis and arm symptoms. Obtain EKG and review prior cardiac studies. Seek emergency assessment promptly for recurrence; additional stress testing may be necessary depending on prior workup and symptoms.
4. Encouraged coordinated care at the facility where the diagnostic records are held; follow-up at this clinic remains available.

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Complex posthospital follow-up for renal dysfunction, edema, suspected vasculitis, diabetes, and anticoagulation.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient is seen after hospitalization and rehabilitation, accompanied by a caregiver who handles much of his medication administration and dietary planning. The course has included difficulty walking, marked leg swelling, renal impairment, rash suspected to represent vasculitis, foot wound infection, and steroid treatment. He is tapering prednisone and was recently treated with Levaquin; continuation of antibiotics after discharge is unclear. The caregiver requests a complete medication list and guidance on a renal, diabetic, and low-sodium diet. The patient has had low systolic blood pressure readings, at times in the 90s. He remains on diuretics and warfarin, with anticoagulation testing previously supervised at the rehabilitation facility. Renal values cited by the family include creatinine near 3.1 and BUN near 47, but the dates and completeness of these results are uncertain.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Chronic or recent significant renal dysfunction, diabetes, edema, suspected vasculitis, anemia, and cardiovascular conditions requiring anticoagulation. A recent infected foot lesion was treated during rehabilitation.

MEDICATIONS: Reconciliation included prednisone taper, furosemide, warfarin, insulin (basal and mealtime doses requiring confirmation), amiodarone, carvedilol, aspirin, calcium, iron, and bowel medications. Uncertain courses of Levaquin were specifically flagged for confirmation with the facility.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: Blood pressure is relatively low. Lungs clear without crackles and heart rhythm regular on auscultation. The foot wound appears improved or healing.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN: Complete pharmacy reconciliation against the rehabilitation discharge list before administering or changing doses. Continue diuresis with close blood pressure, daily weight, swelling, and renal-function monitoring; call for rapid weight gain or worsening hypotension. Check laboratory studies and INR, with anticoagulation clinic referral for warfarin management after facility discharge. Consult rheumatology regarding possible vasculitis and steroid taper, nephrology for renal disease, and cardiology as indicated. Confirm with the treating facility whether further antibiotics are required. Nutrition, dermatology, and sleep evaluation were also coordinated. Caregiver was counseled about follow-up and monitoring.

registros.descripcion: Follow-up for gout and chronic joint symptoms, with concern about nephrotoxicity from longstanding indomethacin use.

Sample Name: Gout, Renal Insufficiency, and Medication Followup

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Follow-up for gout and chronic joint symptoms, with concern about nephrotoxicity from longstanding indomethacin use.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient returns for medication renewals and reports anticipated knee replacement, deferred for personal circumstances. He has longstanding gout and has used indomethacin for approximately 15 years, despite prior discussions about impaired renal function. Last available creatinine was approximately 1.7. A reduced-dose allopurinol regimen and colchicine were introduced previously, yet he continues indomethacin out of concern about recurrent severe attacks. Several other prescriptions, including nasal steroids, lipid-lowering therapy, metoprolol, omeprazole, and thyroid replacement, require reconciliation and renewal. Blood pressure is mildly high at presentation. A prior antihypertensive, valsartan or losartan, is no longer on the active list.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY: Gout, chronic renal insufficiency, hypertension, dyslipidemia, chronic knee disease, and thyroid disease after partial thyroid surgery.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Gout with chronic use of indomethacin and renal impairment. Extensive counseling on progressive kidney risk. Agreed to reduce indomethacin to every other day, then potentially every third day as tolerated, eventually reserving it for short courses during flares. Continue other prescribed urate-lowering and prophylactic therapies with renal considerations.
2. Renal insufficiency. Repeat creatinine and metabolic laboratory tests before further long-term NSAID exposure.
3. Medication refills. Renew appropriate maintenance therapies; do not restart a previously discontinued angiotensin-receptor blocker without review.
4. Check uric acid, thyroid tests, CBC, and other monitoring laboratories. Follow up after laboratory results and at the next routine visit.

Sample Name: Tick Bite and Diabetes Followup

Medical Specialty:

Consult - History and Phy.

Description: Follow-up after an erythema migrans-like tick bite, with uncontrolled blood glucose and medication adjustments.

(Medical Transcription Sample Report)

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient was seen in the emergency department after noticing a red, target-like skin lesion with central clearing following a possible tick bite. He reports no associated fever, malaise, generalized joint pains, chest pain, or respiratory symptoms. Lyme serology is pending. Routine blood count and chemistries were reassuring apart from hyperglycemia. Home morning glucose readings remain approximately 220 to 240 on metformin, and he requests further nutrition or diabetes education. He is awaiting elective evaluation for a deviated nasal septum. He has stopped using an oxygen concentrator due to markedly increased electricity bills but continues CPAP, which he reports helps his sleep. Blood pressure is satisfactory at home. Triglycerides remain elevated and variable despite treatment.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Possible early localized Lyme disease. Complete doxycycline for 14 days, following review of the rash and absence of systemic symptoms. Contact the clinic for new migratory arthralgia, rash, systemic symptoms, or worsening condition while serology is pending.
2. Type 2 diabetes with persistent fasting hyperglycemia. Request renewed diabetes nutrition education and repeat glycemic studies at follow-up.
3. Hypertriglyceridemia. Increase gemfibrozil from once daily to twice daily as discussed, with repeat fasting lipid testing.
4. Hypertension without current edema. Continue metoprolol; furosemide may be held and reserved for recurrent fluid accumulation according to the treating clinician's plan.
5. Sleep-related oxygen. CPAP continued; concentrator use and affordability discussed, but long-term oxygen need requires clinical reassessment rather than assuming no indication.
6. Follow up in approximately three months with repeat laboratory tests.

Description: Evaluation of persistent postnasal drainage, possible parathyroid disease, exertional dyspnea, and hypertension.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: A patient in his early 60s complains of persistent postnasal drainage following dental extractions, intermittent nasal congestion, and progressive shortness of breath with activity including walking and intercourse. He formerly smoked for approximately 25 to 30 years but quit over a decade ago. Prior pulmonary function testing was normal, and prior chest imaging, echocardiography, and stress testing did not identify a definite explanation; he feels exercise tolerance has worsened since those tests. His blood pressure has required medication adjustment, and he wishes to pursue a lower sodium diet and weight reduction. He also has unexplained hypercalcemia and has been told there may be a parathyroid disorder. A previously requested 24-hour urine collection has not yet been completed. He reports loss of muscular endurance and intermittent leg weakness.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION: The clinician hears a possible heart murmur, although a previous echocardiogram did not clearly confirm significant valve pathology. Lungs examined without a definitive new abnormality.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN:
1. Hypercalcemia, possible primary hyperparathyroidism. Complete ordered serum and 24-hour urine studies before choosing medical or surgical treatment.
2. Exertional dyspnea of uncertain cause despite prior reassuring pulmonary and cardiac testing. Repeat echocardiography and seek cardiology evaluation, with additional testing determined by subsequent findings.
3. Hypertension and obesity. Maintain medication adherence and follow low-salt diet, gradual exercise, and weight reduction plan.
4. Postnasal drip. Resume prescribed allergy treatment, including cetirizine, and monitor symptoms.
5. Provide a clear written medication list and follow up in several months.

Repeat a single oral antifungal dose and refer to urology for assessment of persistent lesions and possible need for further investigation or foreskin procedure. No definitive alternative diagnosis or malignancy was established.
2. Excess tearing and intermittent foreign-body sensation. Trial lubricating eye drops; consider ophthalmology review if persistent or progressive.
3. Medication access. Renew appropriate antihypertensive and simvastatin prescriptions with pharmacy pickup as requested.
4. Continue weight reduction efforts and return in approximately four months or sooner if genital symptoms worsen.

3. Multinodular goiter, euthyroid. Endocrinology referral to determine whether ultrasound surveillance or biopsy is warranted; no cancer diagnosis established.
4. Chronic cervical pain. Discussed judicious use of available analgesics without requiring the patient to tolerate uncontrolled pain.
5. Rhinitis. Restart flunisolide, two sprays in each nostril twice daily.
6. Follow up in four to six months, with interim glucose updates by telephone.

Description: Persistent generalized itching without a clear primary rash and request for specialty consultation.

2. Hearing concerns: Arrange hearing evaluation.
3. History of leg edema and cramps: Continue observation and conservative measures as tolerated.
4. Prior cardiac procedure: Reviewed available chart history with the patient.

3. Dental pain with loose filling: Arrange Dental Clinic reassessment for possible extraction.
4. History of stroke: Continue established primary care and rehabilitation follow-up.

4. Gastroesophageal reflux: Renew omeprazole.
5. Constipation: Encourage fluids and dietary fiber.
6. Nocturia and prostate concerns: Discussed screening risks and benefits. No prostate cancer screening was recommended at this encounter given the reported risk profile.

Description: Follow-up for blood pressure, intermittent knee pain, and urgency with occasional stool leakage.

5. Medication renewals: Prescriptions reviewed, including a limited-use medication requiring periodic renewal.

Return in approximately six months or sooner for persistent bowel symptoms.

Description: Ongoing left-sided neuropathic pain with marked anxiety regarding upcoming screening colonoscopy.

1. Left-sided neuropathic pain: Reviewed prior work-up and treatment options. Increase amitriptyline from 25 mg to 50 mg nightly; continue other medications as prescribed.
2. Anxiety surrounding colonoscopy: Provided extensive counseling regarding preparation, sedation and screening rationale. Strongly encouraged keeping the scheduled examination given family history.
3. Recent return to alcohol use: Counseled against using alcohol to manage distress.
4. Hypertension: Mildly elevated reading; continue regimen and monitor.
5. Sleep difficulty and mood complaints: Follow clinical response after medication adjustment.

Medication renewals arranged. Follow up in four months, earlier if symptoms worsen.

Description: Evaluation of depressed mood, intermittent dark stools, worsening respiratory symptoms, and preventive care.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS: The patient reports several weeks of low mood, insomnia, reduced energy, diminished interest, poor concentration, irritability, and weight gain in the setting of significant stress from illnesses affecting both parents. He denies thoughts of harming himself but reports anger toward others. He has noticed black and subsequently green bowel movements, now back to normal color, and intermittent chest and abdominal discomfort.
